sentences.text: Hello, Margaret? It's Priya. Priya Nair, from adult social care. We spoke on the phone on, um, on Monday.
So, if Kevin's here, we can include him, if you're happy with that.
Before we start properly, can I just explain what today is about?
It's basically about understanding how you're managing day to day, what's difficult, what's working, and what matters to you.
And towards the end we look at whether there's any support that would help, and whether you'd be eligible for support from the council.
This isn't about putting you anywhere.
It's about you, here, in your home, and what might make things easier for you.
It'll probably take about an hour, if that's okay with you? And we can stop for a break whenever you want.
So Kevin, that's your son?
And Margaret, that's your wife?
So, thinking about getting about, generally. How are you getting around the house at the moment?
Indoors all the time?
Sometimes I, um, I hold on to the furniture instead. Don't write that down.
And outdoors? Have you been out much since you came home?
Hardly at all. I've got my stick, Frank's old stick actually, for outside.
And the frame, is there one upstairs as well, or do you carry it?
There's a rail on one side. On the right going up.
And coming down's worse because the rail's on the wrong side then, for my right hand, so I sort of go down sideways. Or on my bottom sometimes, if I'm tired.
There's only the one. I leave it at the bottom and I hold on to the wall up top.
There's a rail on one side. On the left going down.
And do you ever get up in the night? To use the toilet, say?
I wear pads at night now. I buy them from the supermarket.
Kevin bought me some with the, um, the velcro, but they're a bit tight.
I used to cook every day. Proper dinners. Frank liked his meat and two veg. Sunday roast, the lot.
I miss the people. I miss Joan and Pat, we always sat together.
I want to stay in my own home. For as long as I possibly can. That's what I want.
I want to have a bath again. I'd love to have a bath again. I'd love it.
I can't push myself up with this wrist. And I think, if I get stuck in there, who's going to find me?
I miss it. I do.
I used to have a bath every night before bed, with my radio on. It was my little treat.
And if at any point you want to talk to me on your own about anything, just say, and that's absolutely fine.
I know it's a big question.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of ending your life?
No. No, love. Not now. Never. I wouldn't. I've got too much to live for, my grandchildren, and Biscuit.
And if things did get very low again, would you feel able to tell someone? Kevin, or Dr Shah?
I'd tell Dr Shah. I think I would. I'd tell Susan, she gets it out of me anyway.
Okay. And if I ever had to go into a home, one day, if it came to that, well, I'd want it to be Beechwood, because Brenda's sister was in there and they were lovely.
But I'm not there yet. Not by a long chalk.
The other thing that will really help straight away is stopping the card. Do you know which bank it is?
So the building society can cancel the card, and issue you a new one with a new PIN. And they can sometimes look into withdrawals as well.
So Kevin, how often are you able to come over?
Two teenagers. And the wife works as well. So it's, yeah. I do what I can.
She's seventy-six herself, Brenda, with her knees. I can't lean on her too much.
She's been thinking about it since about 2010.
She's writing it down. I'm thinking about it.
She's been thinking about it since about 2010.
